articles.title_orig: Justice Department investigating major TV networks over suspending pool coverage of Trump
articles.title_zh: Justice Department investigating major TV networks over suspending pool coverage of Trump
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department said it is investigating five major TV broadcast networks for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, a department spokesperson said.
The investigation into the networks that make up the White House TV press pool — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — is underway, and the department sent out “civil investigative demands” on Friday, according to a Justice Department official.
“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” department spokeswoman Emily Covington said Saturday.
The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording the president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The network performing pool duty then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets.
The New York Times first reported the investigation.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
ABC News said it has not received any notification from the Justice Department but expects to. Representatives for NBC, CBS and CNN declined to comment. Fox did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The investigation appears to be the latest move from the White House in its escalating feud against the press corps.
Last month, Trump barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds, citing what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” The other networks in the TV pool briefly declined to participate in pool duties after CNN was removed from its spot in the rotation.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued to block the ban, claiming it was a violation of the First Amendment. They were reinstated about a week later after a judge ruled that the administration had to temporarily restore their access for 14 days. A federal judge this week extended the order to Tuesday.
The five major networks released a joint statement at the time, saying: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
The pool system has been recognized by administrations from both parties for decades, and the coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which include outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets.
During the time the outlets declined to provide pool coverage, individual TV networks, including NBC News, continued to provide coverage of White House events that were open to the press, outside of the pool.
Bruce D. Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said in a statement that the First Amendment protects the decisions news organizations make about coverage and called the investigation “another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.”
Kelly O’Donnell reported from Washington, and Marlene Lenthang from Los Angeles.
Chief Justice and National Affairs Correspondent
Marlene Lenthang is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Sen. Thom Tillis says he believes Trump’s fuel deal with Russia could be breaking the law
articles.title_zh: Sen. Thom Tillis says he believes Trump’s fuel deal with Russia could be breaking the law
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday that President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia to allow it to release diesel fuel to the global market may be breaking the law.
“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” Tillis said.
Trump announced in a Friday post on Truth Social that Russia would “immediately supply” hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the global marketplace, with more than 1 million additional tons soon on the way. The move drew sharp condemnation from Ukraine and critics of the Trump administration.
Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, lawmakers took a series of steps to try to financially punish the Kremlin. In 2022, the Senate unanimously passed a bill to ban Russian oil imports, and Congress has not made changes to the law to reflect the president’s announcement.
Asked by moderator Kristen Welker whether he believes the president is breaking the law with his Russia deal, Tillis said, “I believe that he may be.”
“We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor,” he added. “Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied.”
The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the senator’s remarks.
Tillis referenced year-end congressional funding negotiations when asked what the Senate could do if Tillis believes Trump is breaking the law.
“If the president wants my support, which I believe he should get for funding military operations and year-end funding beyond baseline funding, I think the president needs to understand this is a problem, and I’m not the only Republican concerned with this,” he said.
Asked whether Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin was putting American lives at risk, Tillis said, “It absolutely will,” pointing to Russian funding of mercenaries and the Kremlin’s relationship with Iran.
Tillis has just months remaining before his term expires. His retirement from the Senate created a high-profile battleground opening. Democrats are eyeing his seat as a prime target to flip as they seek control of the chamber.
Tillis has been highly critical of aspects of the Trump administration, including the performance of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Tillis, who voted for Hegseth’s confirmation, now says he regrets his vote.
Tillis on Sunday condemned the Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted in the 2009 mass shooting in Fort Hood, Texas.
Tillis said that the livestream plans would radicalize people and be used by terrorist groups as a recruiting tool.
“The Fort Hood shooter should be put to death, but there’s a way to deal with this that’s proper, and there’s a way to deal with this that’s more improper than I have ever observed in my life,” he said.
“This is not who we are, and it’s another example of why Pete Hegseth, in all of his bravado, needs to get the hell out of the Department of Defense, because he is a failed leader, and we need strong leadership supporting President Trump right now,” he added.
Megan Brand is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: New York and Pennsylvania's split screen approach to measles
articles.title_zh: New York and Pennsylvania's split screen approach to measles
articles.content_orig:
As predicted when President Donald Trump and his dangerous quack Health Secretary Bobby Kennedy Jr. cast doubt on vaccines, preventable disease is spreading, such as measles.
Now New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has now had to declare a state of emergency over the measles outbreak, which has exceeded 100 cases.
Surprising no one, these cases have been concentrated among rural communities where immunization rates are lower. At least we are not yet in the position of neighboring Pennsylvania, which is struggling with an outbreak of more than 1,000 cases .
Hochul's order will provide some needed state resources and coordination to help overwhelmed counties and localities deal with the repercussions of the spread of a pathogen that is not only extremely contagious but has effects almost no other viruses have, including triggering so-called immune amnesia that can make children and adults more susceptible to other diseases that they'd already developed some immunity against.
It's a shame to have to contend with this in a context where the federal government is not only not a partner, but in some significant ways a driver of the problem.
Kennedy hasn't just used his position to spread his lies, he has taken harmful action, such as with his disastrous decision to stop the routine recommendation of six childhood immunizations, including for influenza, hepatitis, and COVID-19. Attorney General Tish James was right to join 14 other states in filing suit against this decision , which will only harm kids and their families and their communities.
As to measles, each and every case is a policy failure, or sabotage, if you want to look at it like that. This is not a disease that "just happens" or that we simply have to learn to live with until there is effective prevention and treatment. There is effective prevention, and there has been for quite a long time.
It was so effective, in fact, that measles was declared eradicated from the country in the year 2000, ringing in the new millennium with an incredible achievement: no spread at all for a period of 12 months. Put another way, we had cracked the code to having what was once a catastrophe among this nation's children become effectively a non-issue.
To have measles spreading so aggressively again now, a quarter century after this momentous occasion, is not some unfortunate but unavoidable expression of nature, like an earthquake. It is a choice, or rather a series of choices made over time from people ranging from individual parents who refused to get their own children vaccinated to public officials who abdicated their responsibility to protect the public.
The measles virus is not any more dangerous, but the man leading the whole of this country's public health infrastructure is. RFK had already dedicated the bulk of his career to baselessly and aggressively sowing distrust in the accepted medical consensus — rigorously established over decades of research and millions of inoculations — that vaccines are both safe and effective.
He is now using his perch to carry out his agenda, which runs counter to what public health should be. Nature created measles, modern science found the vaccine to stop it cold and end it forever and now horribly, Bobby Kennedy has brought it roaring back.
Every illness and every death is on his and Trump's hands.

articles.title_orig: Chicago Marathon women's wheelchair: Catherine Debrunner sets world record
articles.title_zh: Chicago Marathon women's wheelchair: Catherine Debrunner sets world record
articles.content_orig:
Catherine Debrunner breaks world record at 2026 Bank of America Chicago Marathon,a
Catherine Debrunner is back on top of the Bank of America Chicago Marathon podium -- and continues to be on top of the world.
The fierce Swiss wheelchair racer, who won the race in 2024, just soared to victory at the 2026 competition, shattering her own world record in the process.
Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
Debrunner set the world record in 2023 when she finished the Berlin Marathon in 1 hour, 34 minutes and 16 seconds. She finished Sunday in 1:33:16 -- exactly one minute faster.
"I don't think we have ever seen anything like this," analyst, Olympian and former Chicago Marathon champion  Amanda McGrory said during the NBC Chicago broadcast of the race. "This is a historical event we're seeing right now."
Debrunner has now won 12 major marathons, including in her U.S. debut in Chicago in 2023 and again in 2024.
The victory comes after she finished runner-up at the 2026 Boston Marathon earlier this year before capturing her fourth London Marathon title.
"I really gave all I could and when I saw the time at the finish … it felt great. It's unbelievable," Debrunner said after her victory.
Debrunner said she didn't enter the race expecting a world record, but credited the crowd and the conditions with helping her to a victory.
"I just wanted to give all I could, and that's what I did," she said.
Debrunner's victory came as defending Chicago women’s wheelchair champion Susannah Scaroni took the 2026 race off to welcome her first child.
Debrunner finished well ahead of a strong group of contenders, many of whom have won the division since 2015, including nine-time champion Tatyana McFadden and two-time champion Manuela Schär. McFadden finished second in a sprint to the finish with Schär.
Check back for more on this developing story.

articles.title_orig: Threats of Political Violence Have America’s Elected Officials Living in Fear
articles.title_zh: Threats of Political Violence Have America’s Elected Officials Living in Fear
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Capitol steps.  (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Violent threats targeted at least 70 U.S. senators, 185 House members, and 44 governors over the past two years, a New York Times investigation found, as candidates enter the final weeks of the midterm campaign.
The Times culled its tally from more than 100 open-records requests, court files, and law enforcement logs covering 2024 through August.
The threats hit Republicans and Democrats alike and reached more than half of the nation's secretaries of state, most of whom oversee their states' elections.
Official figures agree. The U.S. Capitol Police, which protects Congress, investigated 14,938 cases involving concerning statements, behaviors, and communications aimed at lawmakers, their families, staff, and the Capitol in 2025, up from 9,474 in 2024, a nearly 58% increase.
Yet the Times identified only 53 federal cases over the two years in which someone was charged with threatening a public official other than the president.
Former Capitol Police Chief J. Thomas Manger told the paper that fewer than 10% of the cases his investigators handled in 2021 resulted in charges.
Vague statutes, free-speech protections, and anonymous senders make many cases difficult to prosecute.
The cost shows up in campaign ledgers. Federal candidates spent roughly $6 million on security in the 2017-2018 election cycle and at least $25 million in the current cycle through Aug. 1, more than four times the earlier total, the Times reported , citing campaign finance records. That excludes officials' personal spending.
In Indiana, Rodric Bray, the Republican leader of the state Senate, became a chief target after his chamber voted 31-19 last December to reject a congressional map backed by President Donald Trump.
The plan aimed to eliminate the state's two Democratic-held congressional districts. At least 12 elected Republicans in Indiana faced threats or swatting attempts — false emergency reports intended to send armed police to a target's home — NBC News reported.
Bray, who plans to step down from his leadership post in November election, told the Times that bomb and death threats targeted his office and home, and he began varying his daily routine.
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., who left Congress in January after breaking with Trump over the release of files on convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, said in a May speech that when she texted Trump about threats aimed at her son, he told her "that it was my fault, and I deserve it," CBS News reported .
The White House did not deny the message's contents, the Times reported; spokesman Davis Ingle said Trump condemns political violence.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., drew a wave of threats last November after posting a video with five other lawmakers telling troops they need not obey unlawful orders, a message Trump branded seditious.
Someone swatted her parents' home while her father was dying of cancer, Slotkin said. "I signed up for this, but my family and my staff did not," she told the paper.
Capitol Police Chief Michael Sullivan told House appropriators in March that threats against Congress in 2026 were on pace to exceed the 2025 total, the Times reported .

The projects celebrate the legendary singer's rags-to-rhinestones legacy. Fans express emotional reactions to the immersive experience, sharing how they can feel her presence throughout the new building.
Kelly Clarkson is calling out a Brooklyn store after she claimed an employee mistreated her.
On Saturday, the singer and talk show host took to X to share details of her recent experience at Art of Play, a store known for its collection of toys, games, books, puzzles and other unique items.
"Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson wrote.

Kelly Clarkson described a recent shopping experience to one of Julia Roberts' character in "Pretty Woman." (Getty Images)

Clarkson then compared the encounter to a memorable scene from the 1990 film "Pretty Woman," in which Julia Roberts’ character, Vivian Ward, is dismissed by a boutique saleswoman who assumes she cannot afford the store’s clothing.
MICHAEL DOUGLAS' WILDEST HOLLYWOOD CONFESSIONS: FROM A-LIST ACTRESS BITE TO JULIA ROBERTS CLASH
"But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in ‘Pretty Woman.’ For sure, check it out," Clarkson added.

Clarkson’s post quickly drew attention from her followers, some of whom defended the singer and criticized the store on social media. Several users also appeared to leave negative reviews on the business’ Google listing.

articles.title_orig: The Greatest Bull Market in Decades is About to Begin – But a Correction Comes First
articles.title_zh: The Greatest Bull Market in Decades is About to Begin – But a Correction Comes First
articles.content_orig:
For investors who think they’ve missed out on AI, the best is yet to come. But first, there will be a notable correction.
Since March 2009, the S&P 500 has experienced five declines of roughly 20% or more. Most were followed by relatively quick recoveries, reinforcing the belief that “buying the dip” is a reliable long-term strategy. However, these declines occurred within a broader secular bull market, which is an important distinction.
Understanding the secular trend often matters more than stock picking, as even the very best stocks can see extended periods of volatility if the secular trend reverses. In this report, we compare the current bull market to secular trends going back over 150 years to show why it is an extreme outlier.
Precisely because this market is an extreme outlier, how investors position themselves over the next few years will be crucial, particularly in AI stocks. My firm, the I/O Fund, specializes in AI, and while past performance is not a guarantee of future results, our track record in AI stocks has been exceptional.
Below, we do what very few investors dare to do, which is share our game plan and explain why we believe this bull market has considerably more room to run. However, before the next leg higher begins, we expect a correction that will shake many investors out of the trade.
The current bull market has lasted 17 years, and history proves this is very rare. Typically, long secular bull markets are broken up by periods of consolidation; but for more than a decade, that has not been the case.
The data shows that going back as far as 1880, there have been seven secular bear markets. They lasted, on average, 6.7 years with an average drawdown of 52.7%.
By comparison, since 1880, the average secular bull market lasts 11.2 years, with an average gain of 675%.
Compare this to the current bull market, going for 17.4 years old and up 1,073%, as of September 2026. On both measures it is becoming an extreme outlier compared to the average. That alone calls for caution, because it suggests we are closer to the end of this secular trend than the beginning. However, late in the cycle doesn’t mean over, and the wave structure outlined below shows why.
The Elliott Wave pattern of the current secular advance supports this view. Since the 2009 low, the market has been tracing a standard five-wave pattern, which follows the same guidelines on all time frames.
Below are some data points to support this claim:
Regarding the last point just made, an ending diagonal is a common pattern in Elliott Wave analysis, and the most likely interpretation of where we are in the larger secular pattern that started in 2009. These patterns only show up at the beginning and end of a trend, and they have distinct characteristics: they are 5 wave patterns, have exceptional overlap, and tend to trace a trend channel.
With those features in mind, I am tracking two scenarios that best fit the current price action.
The bigger takeaways from this analysis are twofold:
The above count aligns with what we’ve been seeing across AI stocks over the past year. Many of our positions are showing technical setups that point to longer, secular uptrends, with the potential for years of upside despite periods of volatility. Below, we examine Memory stocks – one of the hottest trends in AI to see whether the charts support a continued uptrend.
The South Korean KOSPI, an index consisting of 942 stocks, just dropped 44% in less than one month. This is a remarkable move for a developed country’s broad market, and there were several dynamics that created an environment for this unprecedented drop, one of which is that 54% of the total allocation of the index was Samsung and SK Hynix.
Even with the extraordinary volatility that we saw in the South Korean markets, the uptrend in this economy appears to be incomplete. As one of the primary beneficiaries to the memory boom needed to scale AI, this makes sense from a narrative perspective, as there is no evidence the need for memory is over, especially as we move into the inference phase of AI.
Get weekly stock insights, market analysis, and technology updates straight to your inbox.
The KOSPI hit the lower target where we typically see 4 th waves end. If this level breaks, we can still be in an extended 4 th wave decline which has ample room to drop and still maintain the integrity of the larger secular uptrend.
Micron is in direct, aggressive competition with Samsung and SK Hynix for HBM orders. Interestingly, it’s long-term chart resembles the South Korean Kospi, almost identically.
We cover AI setups in detail during our weekly webinars, including the key levels we’re watching and how we’re positioning the portfolio. Join the I/O Fund’s next webinar at 4:30 p.m. Eastern on Thursday to see what the charts are signaling for AI stocks. Join I/O Fund
This is an area of the AI stack that we are heavily overweight – just over 50% of our portfolio is tilted toward lesser-known names that are directly involved in solving the networking bottleneck in AI.
One name that we have been vocal about, which is up over 188% YTD as one of our top 3 positions, is Lumentum (LITE) . Like memory, LITE, which sits in the middle of the networking stack, appears to have several large swings in its future.
Our firm was one of the first to address the AI energy bottleneck in 2024 . As a result, the I/O Fund used a portion of the cash we raised in early 2025 to buy Bloom Energy (BE) on the April 2025 lows. This caused our firm to establish a 5% allocation at $16.88 that is currently up over 1600%.
Bloom Energy addresses a very different challenge in the AI infrastructure buildout than networking or memory, yet its technical chart is signaling a similar long-term opportunity. Our analysis suggests Bloom is in the middle of a large five-wave pattern, with the potential for several more years of upside before the cycle is complete.
On a shorter timeframe, the S&P 500 appears to be setting up for a high of some kind into this cycle window. We appear to be tracing a smaller diagonal into this window, as shown below.
The breakout to all-time highs has confirmed this patterns completion. At minimum, we would then expect a pullback to the 7,300–7,265 area. If 7,265 breaks, the next target is 7,000–6,683.
This alternative scenario is outlined in red and is simply a different way to count the bullish scenario. Instead of a very shallow wave 2 happening in early June, which is what the green count is listing, we would be in that wave 2 once the 7265 support breaks. That would be uncomfortable, but as long as 6,683 holds, both outcomes would be pullbacks within a larger bullish uptrend. Below 6,683 and the odds will increase that we are setting up for the larger 4 th wave drop targeting sub-6000.
The important AI proxy in the broad semiconductor ETF (SMH) is confirming this risk. It is finishing a three-wave bounce on weak volume. Because the bounce made a lower high, it is best counted as a B wave in an ongoing correction, and not confirming the push higher in the S&P 500. A break below $541 would confirm this view, with a final target of $470–$430. A break above $640–$671.83 would invalidate the downside setup and point to a more bullish outcome sooner.
Our analysis of the AI investment cycle, combined with strength in the U.S. economy, suggests the secular bull market has another 1-3 years to run. While the current cycle is mature, we believe some of the strongest gains may still be ahead. We will especially watch key levels, such as 6,683 on the S&P 500 to ensure our strategy remains unchanged.
However, the path will not be without volatility. A strengthening U.S. dollar could tighten global liquidity conditions, which we will review in next week’s article. We would view that weakness as a potential buying opportunity, particularly for lesser-known AI stocks, which we cover weekly in our 1-hour webinars held every Thursday at 4:30 p.m. Eastern.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia Has Few Options as Houthis Aim at Heart of Its Ambitions
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia Has Few Options as Houthis Aim at Heart of Its Ambitions
articles.content_orig:
As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis continue to wreak havoc on the kingdom.
The kingdom launched a major offensive last week to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis, but the rebels have so far held their ground.
Instead, they have escalated their campaign against the kingdom, culminating in Saturday’s missile attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 12 people.
Drawing from Iran’s playbook in its conflict with the United States, the Houthis are vowing a painful escalation, targeting critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and imposing a global economic cost.
The Houthis have longstanding grievances against Saudi Arabia over Riyadh’s decade-long war against the group, which triggered the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. The recent Houthi escalation, however, is increasingly seen as an extension of Iran’s conflict with Washington.
After eleven years of trying to contain the Houthi advance militarily and through talks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khaled bin Salman, face limited options. Across the border, the rebels have grown more powerful, consolidating control over major cities and pushing to seize others, such as the densely populated Taiz.
“This threat has to be dealt with once and for all,” Ali Shihabi, an author and commentator on Saudi politics told CNN. “A lot will depend on the performance of the Yemeni government troops on the ground and Saudi is helping them extensively with air power.”
So far , Saudi Arabia has largely confined its role to providing air cover for the anti-Houthi Yemeni coalition, stopping short of any major deployment of its own troops on the ground. Whether that restraint will hold after Saturday’s strike on Riyadh remains an open question.
Sending large numbers of Saudi troops into Yemen would plunge the kingdom into a an expensive and grinding ground war across rugged terrain and undercut the image Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is carefully cultivating of a stable, investment-friendly kingdom and global tourism hub.
Barely two decades ago, the Houthis were little more than a small religious revivalist movement. With Iranian backing, they have since grown into a formidable fighting force in possession of ballistic missiles and capable of striking as far away as Tel Aviv.
“They’ve developed their warfare,” a southern Yemeni official who fought the Houthis for years told CNN. “They’ve gotten more sophisticated in their attacks, they’re persistent and they’ve enhanced their intelligence.”
Yemen’s government alleges that Houthi rebels have worked with Iranian Revolutionary Guard experts to modify missiles into more effective weapons.
The new missiles fly faster and use a thermal-tracking system to home in on any heat source, Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemen’s armed forces, said. It remains unclear whether such missiles were used during Saturday’s attack on Riyadh airport.
The Houthis’ pursuit of more sophisticated weapons may now be extending into artificial intelligence.
AI company Anthropic said a group based in northern Yemen used its Claude AI tools to help develop guidance software for rockets and missiles – the systems that steer and stabilize the weapons in flight. The report did not identify those involved, but their location in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen suggests a possible link to the rebels.
Saudi Arabia has sought support from partners across the world to counter the group. France, Britain and Pakistan have committed support, while other allies like Turkey are considering sending help.
Prince Mohammed has also reportedly turned to Syria for help. Its president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had led armed factions that successfully drove Iranian-backed groups from Syria after nearly a decade of civil war.
Yet Riyadh’s biggest ally, the US, has not supported air strikes on the Houthis, instead sending more than 100 military advisers to provide intelligence under a newly formed joint command.
Last year Washington reached a ceasefire with the Iran-backed group that reopened the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the maritime chokepoint through which global trade flows between Asia and Europe, to US vessels. Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month , urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but the president declined to intervene.
How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen
“Clearly, direct US involvement via air power would help because US aircraft can respond to US satellite intelligence more rapidly,” Shihabi said. “Saudi aircraft… are one stop removed from that loop so US involvement would be helpful.”
Saudi Arabia, one of the largest countries in the Middle East, remains vulnerable despite procuring some of the most advanced US air defenses. Its infrastructure, which carries rich resources across vast desert terrain, leaves it an easy target for the cheaper one-way drones developed by the Houthis.
Among those killed in the Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport was an American citizen, the Saudi civil aviation body said Sunday – an attack that might draw Trump further into the war.
“The Saudis are good fighters,” Trump told reporters following the attack. “But I think the attack was a terrible thing.”
Asked whether the US will join strikes on the Houthis, the US president said: “We may”

articles.title_orig: World leaders condemn Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
articles.title_zh: World leaders condemn Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
articles.content_orig:
An attack by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport drew condemnation from European leaders, the United Nations and regional governments on Sunday.
The attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport prompted warnings to travelers, expressions of solidarity with Saudi Arabia and calls for an end to attacks on civilian infrastructure.
International condemnation of Houthi attack
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Iran-backed Houthi forces are destabilizing regional transport and energy infrastructure.
“These attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen said.
She described the airport strike as a dangerous escalation and called for an immediate end to attacks on civilians.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas also condemned the strike, calling it an “appalling act of terror.”
“There can be no justification for indiscriminate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure,” Kallas said.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for an immediate halt to attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.
“Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law,” Guterres said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul described the strike as “a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation,” while British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband urged British nationals to avoid Riyadh airport and follow Saudi authorities' instructions.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni censured the attack and expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and the victims' families.
“Attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure are unacceptable and must stop,” Meloni wrote on X.
Meloni said Italy would continue working with regional partners to promote stability and freedom of navigation.
France also condemned the attack, describing it as “heinous” and expressing its “total solidarity” with Saudi Arabia, the French Foreign Ministry said on Sunday.
France would continue supporting Saudi Arabia in defending its territory and infrastructure, including through its military assistance, the ministry said. It also called on the Houthis to immediately stop attacks and provocations destabilizing the region.
Russia also condemned the attack on Riyadh's international airport, Interfax news agency reported on Sunday.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned the attack and offered condolences to the families of those killed.
“There can be no justification for attacks on civilian infrastructure,” Carney said.
The Arab League and Syria also condemned the strike. Syria's Foreign Ministry said a Syrian citizen had been killed and called for international action to prevent further attacks on civilian facilities.
Pakistan reaffirmed its commitment to Saudi Arabia's security under the two countries' joint defense agreement.
“Pakistan stands in unwavering solidarity with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its leadership and brotherly people,” Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said.
The Houthis subsequently renewed their warning to airlines, airport workers and travelers against using Saudi airports, saying Saudi Arabia bore responsibility for failed interceptions.
Iranian officials warn of further military action
Separately, Iranian officials warned against further attacks on Iran and reiterated threats over the Strait of Hormuz.
An adviser to the commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said that any new attack involving missiles or aircraft would trigger a stronger Iranian response.
“Any provocation or attack with missiles or aircraft will be met with a heavier and crushing response,” Mohammad Reza Naghdi said on Sunday.
Iranian Army Deputy Coordinator Habibollah Sayyari said the military had previously struck vessels and remained prepared to do so again.
“We defended firmly and will continue to do so,” Sayyari said. “Wherever necessary, we will act to strike the enemy.”
Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said that Iran's response to any new military action would differ from its previous responses.
“Our response in the 40-day war was different from the 12-day war, and we hope our adversaries will show some rationality,” Gharibabadi said.
Gharibabadi also described the Strait of Hormuz as an Iranian waterway and said the country would use it as an instrument against its adversaries.
Lawmaker Hassan Ghashghavi said support for reviewing Iran's nuclear doctrine was growing among officials, experts and the public.
Ghashghavi also argued that Iran's control over the Strait of Hormuz was strengthening and that the waterway could not reopen until the Islamic Republic's conditions were met.
Separately, the newspaper Khorasan, which is close to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, wrote that Washington and Israel had already decided to launch another war and that recent diplomatic exchanges were unlikely to alter that decision.
Nuclear dispute and maritime pressure continue
Atomic Energy Organization of Iran chief Mohammad Eslami criticized international institutions and the International Atomic Energy Agency for their response to attacks on Iranian nuclear and non-nuclear facilities.
“The silence and selective approach of international institutions and the IAEA toward direct attacks on the Islamic Republic’s nuclear and non-nuclear facilities represent an obvious and disastrous contradiction in the international system,” Eslami said.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi separately maintained that US-Israeli strikes on Iranian oil and energy infrastructure had created environmental hazards, including the possible contamination of air, soil and water.
Maritime developments added another dimension to the day's security concerns.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported an encounter involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman, hours after the US military announced that it had struck a vessel attempting to breach its naval blockade of Iran.
The agency advised vessels to remain alert as authorities examined the circumstances.
The international condemnation of the Houthi attack on Riyadh airport came alongside renewed threats from the Houthis and Iranian officials, raising concerns about further attacks on civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping across the region.
The discussion, hosted by Fardad Farahzad, brought together Kerri Bitsoff, a former senior official at the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC); Patrick Clawson, the Morningstar senior fellow at the Washington Institute; and Mohammad Machine-Chian, a senior economist and analyst at Iran International.
“The thing about sanctions, if they’re on the books but not enforced, they only hurt the people,” Bitsoff said, arguing that the current US campaign differed from previous rounds by focusing more heavily on enforcement and the financial intermediaries sustaining Iran’s economy.
Iran faces declining oil revenues alongside damage to its energy infrastructure following the war, raising the prospect of severe economic difficulties during the coming winter, Clawson said.
President Masoud Pezeshkian had acknowledged that Iran could not export oil during the initial blockade, according to Clawson, who said the country subsequently sought alternative routes for limited shipments.
Iran had also relied on oil previously stored aboard vessels and in China, but those reserves were approaching exhaustion, he said.
Damage to natural gas infrastructure could compound the difficulties, potentially forcing greater reliance on mazut, a heavily polluting fuel used for electricity generation.
Iran depends on natural gas for approximately 69 percent of its energy requirements, making disruptions particularly consequential for households and industry, Clawson said.
Machine-Chian estimated that between $21 and $23 billion in export proceeds had not returned to Iran and that the blockade could cost the country another $35 billion in oil rev

articles.title_orig: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Welcome Home’ event
articles.title_zh: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Welcome Home’ event
articles.content_orig:
Get ready for a smart home hub, a refreshed HomePod Mini, a faster Apple TV, and maybe some LG smart locks.
Get ready for a smart home hub, a refreshed HomePod Mini, a faster Apple TV, and maybe some LG smart locks.
We are quickly coming up on Apple’s “ Welcome Home ” launch event, where we expect a host of smart home-related announcements. We are expecting refreshes to Apple TV and HomePod Mini, as well as a brand new smart home hub . We could also see the debut of a new platform called homeOS, and some partner devices from LG.
What we probably won’t be seeing is the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook, which Cupertino whisperer Mark Gurman says will debut later this month .
“Welcome Home” will officially kick off in New York on October 13th at 9AM ET. Here’s more about what to expect.
Until now, Apple has primarily relied on the Home app to control all the various bits and bobs that make up your smart home. But it’s a market niche that the company has been eager to tackle more fully . The new device , which could be called HomePad or HomeView or, more simply, Apple Home Hub, will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touchscreen that can either be mounted on a wall or placed on a table or countertop. According to Mark Gurman, the countertop model will somewhat resemble the iMac G4, with the screen attached to an arm set into a half sphere.
It will also supposedly use voice or facial recognition to identify who is interacting with it, pulling up the relevant contacts, calendar appointments, and more. Apple will offer the option for secondary identification through an iPhone to keep personal data more secure. The whole thing will reportedly run a new software platform called…
The company may have registered a trademark for the name through a shell company called Home Operations Suite LLC, a move that Apple has pulled before to quietly secure the rights to names. The platform will supposedly feature a streamlined interface that “looks like a mashup of iOS, tvOS and watchOS,” according to Gurman . The focus, obviously, will be on smart home applications, like controlling thermostats and smart locks, and it will also be capable of making FaceTime calls.
The OS will also include your usual assortment of Apple apps and widgets, including Apple Music, Podcasts, and News, as well as Reminders, Notes, and Siri AI.
Word is that not much is changing with the HomePod Mini or Apple TV. The designs will remain the same, but they’ll get a new processor to help handle the added demand of Siri AI. This will be the first update to the HomePod Mini since it was announced on October 13th of 2020 — exactly six years before Apple’s Welcome Home event. While the company isn’t making any dramatic changes for the Mini’s birthday, it will be offering it in new colors, including green and pink.
This will be the first hardware refresh for the Apple TV since 2022. In addition to supporting Siri AI, the new processor will also speed up navigation, which can get a bit laggy. Both are expected to feature Apple’s N1 chip, which includes support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 6.0.
It’s likely that we’ll get a mention of products that integrate with HomeKit and offer new features built on top of homeOS and whatever Apple’s hardware hub ends up being called. But don’t expect Apple to share too much of the spotlight with its partners . We’ve already seen a leak of LG smart home, including deadbolts, thermostats, and more . They’ll also reportedly include an NFC-based “ Proximity Control ” that pops up a hint in the iPhone’s Dynamic Island when held near the device, as well as a “ tap to set up without power ” pairing feature.

The World Bank Group is Leading the Charge for Private Capital Mobilization in Nigeria
https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/feature/2026/10/11/unlocking-5-79-billion-world-bank-group-private-capital-mobilization-nigeria
This effort reflects a coordinated World Bank Group approach. The World Bank supports reforms and projects that improve the investment environment and create viable opportunities. IFC complements this work by structuring investments, deploying its own capital, and bringing commercial lenders and institutional investors into those opportunities. MIGA provides guarantees that reduce risks for investors. Together, the institutions are helping make private investment a stronger driver of infrastructure, productivity, and jobs.
Since mid-2023, Nigeria has undertaken reforms to improve foreign-exchange management, strengthen public finances, reform fuel subsidies, and create more predictable conditions for investment. Supported in part by the World Bank’s RESET and NAIJA development policy financing programs, these measures are helping strengthen policy credibility. Further reforms aim to deepen capital markets, expand digital trade, enable greater private participation in electricity, and improve competitiveness—reducing risks and opening new opportunities for private capital.
Reforms can open the door to investment, but their impact is felt only when capital begins to flow into projects that change people’s lives. Across digital infrastructure, agriculture, and finance for small businesses, World Bank Group-supported projects and investment platforms are translating improved conditions into concrete opportunities for private capital.
In the digital sector, the Building Resilient Digital Infrastructure for Growth (BRIDGE) Project represents a new model for infrastructure development. Instead of relying solely on public financing, the project will use a public-private partnership to build, own, and operate a nationwide open-access fiber-optic network. The first round of investor selection is expected to mobilize at least $156 million in private equity, while subsequent financing rounds could unlock up to $1.1 billion in private investment by 2030.
The scale of that investment is matched by the reach of its potential impact. BRIDGE will bring affordable broadband access to an additional 58 million people, expanding coverage from 92 million people in 2025 to 150 million by 2030. The beneficiaries include an additional 42 million young people and 15 million women. The project will also connect millions of households, 38,800 public schools, 16,900 health facilities, and 3,400 local government offices to high-speed broadband internet—bringing connectivity closer to the places where people learn, seek care, access public services, and build livelihoods.
For Nigeria’s farmers, limited access to quality seeds, affordable fertilizer, digital services, and reliable markets constrains productivity and incomes. The World Bank Group’s AgriConnect approach links public-sector reforms and investment platforms with IFC financing to address these barriers across agricultural value chains. The Agricultural Value Chains for Growth (AGROW) Project targets one million smallholder farmers, including women and young people, by improving seed and fertilizer systems, strengthening digital platforms, increasing transparency, and expanding links to markets. AGROW is expected to mobilize approximately $220 million from agribusiness firms and a further $22 million from certified seed producers. These interventions are intended to reduce investment risks, strengthen food security and productivity, and create more reliable opportunities for farmers and agribusinesses.
The Fostering Inclusive Finance for MSMEs in Nigeria program (FINCLUDE) is designed to expand the availability and quality of finance for more than 250,000 micro, small, and medium enterprises in job-intensive sectors, with 30 percent of financing targeted to women-led businesses. A $500 million package from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association combines financing and risk-sharing tools to encourage financial institutions and other investors to provide additional capital to underserved firms. The program is expected to mobilize nearly $1.89 billion in private financing and support an estimated 850,000 direct and indirect jobs.
Creating stronger agricultural value chains requires both better systems for farmers and investment in the businesses that supply the inputs they need. Building on the World Bank-supported platforms described above, IFC is helping turn viable opportunities into investments—using direct financing, partnerships with other lenders, and capital-markets instruments to mobilize additional private capital at scale.
In support of the broader AgriConnect agenda, IFC financing for Dangote Industries Limited and Indorama Fertilizer is helping expand domestic fertilizer production and improve access to inputs for more than 10 million smallholder farmers. IFC helped mobilize $1.02 billion for Dangote through refinancing and financing from development institutions and commercial lenders, and $282.5 million for Indorama through syndicated financing. With an aggregate production capacity of 6.8 million metric tons per year, the two projects can reduce reliance on imported inputs, improve affordability, and strengthen food security. Together with AGROW, these investments show how reforms, public programs, and private financing can reinforce different parts of the same agricultural value chain.
The same approach—using IFC participation to draw in private investors and expand essential infrastructure—is also advancing Nigeria’s digital transformation. In telecommunications, IFC served as an anchor investor in a $1.2 billion bond issuance by IHS Towers, helping mobilize more than $1.1 billion from private investors and broaden participation in the transaction. The issuance demonstrated investor confidence not only in Nigeria’s digital infrastructure sector but also in the country’s capital markets. Through its tower-sharing model, IHS Towers enables mobile network operators to expand connectivity more quickly and at lower cost while reducing the environmental footprint of network deployment.
Taken together, these examples show how the World Bank Group’s institutions contribute distinct but complementary tools. Policy reforms improve the enabling environment; investment projects and platforms create viable opportunities; IFC helps structure and mobilize financing around them; and MIGA can mitigate risks that deter investors. This sequencing helps public resources catalyze larger pools of private capital while maintaining a clear focus on development impact.
Together, these reforms, platforms, guarantees, and investments are helping mobilize up to $5.79 billion in private financing in fiscal year 2026. The significance of that figure lies in what it can deliver: more affordable broadband, stronger agricultural value chains, better access to finance for small businesses, and more opportunities for women and young people. It demonstrates how scarce public resources can reduce risk, attract private investment, and support job-rich growth at scale.
As reforms advance and investment opportunities expand, the significance of this coordinated approach will be measured not only in capital mobilized, but in what that capital makes possible: farmers reaching stronger markets, businesses gaining room to grow, communities connecting to essential services, and more women and young people finding pathways to opportunity. By helping close infrastructure and financing gaps, the World Bank Group is supporting a more resilient, productive, and private sector-led Nigerian economy.

articles.title_orig: 'SNL' Cold Open Skewers Pete Hegseth & RFK Jr.'s USS Lincoln Speeches
articles.title_zh: 'SNL' Cold Open Skewers Pete Hegseth & RFK Jr.'s USS Lincoln Speeches
articles.content_orig:
Saturday Night Live ‘s cold open skewered Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in an unhinged takedown.
On Saturday, October 10, SNL took aim at President Donald Trump ‘s cabinet members as Hegseth ( Colin Jost ) and RFK Jr. ( James Austin Johnson ) gave speeches to sailors on the USS Lincoln, who recently completed a 322-day deployment.
The cold open kicked off with Hegseth walking out with an ammo belt made of Fireball Cinnamon Whiskey bottles.
“I’m honored to be here addressing all you brave men…and women,” Hegseth said, before asking the Navy service members how they were doing.
After one sailor pointed out, “We’re bad,” Hegseth replied, “OK, I heard ‘awesome.'”
The secretary of war added. “After seven months at war, you’re back home safe at sunny San Diego, which the president just asked Iran to blow up. I couldn’t be more proud of you. Only eight of you attempted suicide, two of you since I started talking. You executed over 3,000 combat missions, and you did it with zero casualties, zero flight mishaps, and zero working toilets.”
Next, Hegseth briefed the sailors on what they have missed on land.
“In December, as we get into the Christmas spirit, we’re gonna execute a guy in a wheelchair on live TV,” he announced. “Yeah, that’s right, public executions are back. Kinda like Scrubs . And if the guy somehow survives the firing squad, then he’s got to fight Jake Paul .”
Hegseth also said that he recently unveiled the new logo for the Department of War.
“Sorry, is that a Nazi eagle?” one sailor asked, to which Hegseth explained, “It’s an American eagle with a Nazi vibe.”
The same sailor insisted, “Yeah, it just looks identical to the Nazi eagle,” prompting Hegseth to fire back, “Yeah, the only eagle you should be worried about is your mom spread-eagle on my bed right now.”
That’s when RFK Jr. took the podium to address the sailors.
“I’m happy to report that America is healthier than ever,” Johnson, doing his best RFK Jr. impression, proclaimed. “That’s why I would officially like to rename cold and flu season to cold and flue and listeria and measles and trench brain season. We’re also looking into something called testicular dementia.”
Additionally, RFK Jr. acknowledged that 200,000 pounds of pork, beef, and goat had been recalled, pointing out, “But I just want to stress that catfish, pony, and cricket are viable proteins for any American family.”
He also thanked the sailors for testing the meat on them before speaking gibberish, prompting Hegseth to slap him on the back and cause him to speak clearly.
To end the address, Hegseth sang a portion of Linkin Park’s “In the End” and expressed gratitude for the sailors.
“Thank you for all being willing to go down with the ship, even though it breaks my personal rule of never going down on anyone,” he said. “And live from New York, it’s Saturday Night !”

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Simon pounds resorts and vulnerable towns along Mexico’s Pacific coast
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Simon pounds resorts and vulnerable towns along Mexico’s Pacific coast
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Simon's eye remains just off Mexico's Pacific coast, but the Category 4 storm's most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.
Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center said it's not clear if it will make landfall. This could mean Simon maintains its extremely dangerous strength, sustaining winds of 150 mph.
That's not good news for people in the Puerto Vallarta area, a popular destination for U.S. tourists. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.
At daybreak, Simon was centered about 110 miles south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, and moving north-northwest at a relatively slow 6 mph. A senior hurricane center specialist, Phillipe Pappin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico was the most likely place for landfall.
"Simon is very close to the coast of Mexico this morning," Pappin told The Associated Press on Sunday.
"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Pappin said. "They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."
Meanwhile, the hurricane was dumping rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 10 to 20 inches of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches.
Jalisco state suspended classes on Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas.
On Saturday, ahead of the storm's arrival, convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows. Few were walking the streets under overcast skies.
"Let's hope it doesn't hit us, right? That it doesn't affect us," Jesús Gómez said as he stood outside a shop and handed out free samples of candied peanuts to passersby. "We'll be working as usual throughout the day, but when Civil Protection officials come and tell us we need to close, then we'll close and take shelter until the storm passes."
The hurricane center expected a dangerous storm surge "along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall." The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.
Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who, along with his wife, still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.
"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do Saturday. "I just don't know what to expect."
Unlike the Atlantic, which saw just its first named hurricane of the season this week with Isaias, the Pacific season has been very active. Simon's arrival comes on the heels of Polo , which slammed Mexico last week as a Category 2 hurricane before reaching the southwestern U.S. and bringing heavy flooding to the region.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he is 'going to look at' joining Saudi Arabia in the fight against Iran-backed Houthis after deadly airport strike
articles.title_zh: Trump says he is 'going to look at' joining Saudi Arabia in the fight against Iran-backed Houthis after deadly airport strike
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said he is considering joining Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen after a deadly attack on Riyadh's main airport, a move that could draw the U.S. further into a second front in the Iran war .
"We may. We're going to look at it," Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday when asked if the U.S. would back Saudi Arabian strikes. "We just found out about the recent attack. So, we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
Two Saudi Arabian government officials told MS NOW that the kingdom is requesting "urgent defense support" from the U.S. following the attacks.
The officials, including a senior member of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, did not want to be identified because of the matter's sensitivity. They added that the U.S. needs to intervene "as soon as possible" to help the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen fight the Houthis.
The White House did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.
On Sunday, a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the Riyadh airport, one day after a missile struck the same terminal, the Associated Press reported. No immediate details were available about the latest strike on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, AP said.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said Saturday's attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the country's official Saudi Gazette media outlet reported .
Colonel Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, which has been leading the fight against the Houthis, described the attack as a "war crime."
"Therefore, the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will respond decisively to this terrorist attack in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law," Al-Maliki said in a post on X.
It was the second deadly assault on Riyadh's airport in less than a week.
Three Saudi nationals, including a pilot , were killed in attacks on the facility by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Thursday.
Following Saturday's attack, the Houthis renewed their warning against using Saudi airports.
"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using ⁠Saudi ‌airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become ⁠a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina," the Houthis said in a post on X.
Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally in the Middle East, intervened in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and its internationally recognized government after the group seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in 2014.
Last month, the Trump administration approved the potential $24.3 billion sale of nearly 50 F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia in what was seen as a major boost for the kingdom as it faces intensifying attacks from the Houthis. The sale is under congressional review.
The Saudi energy ministry said a long-planned international energy conference will still take place in Riyadh on Sunday, Reuters reported.
The five-day WPC Energy Congress ⁠is taking place at a convention center near King Khalid airport. State television told Reuters that more than 70 ministers, ⁠300 company executives and representatives of more than 25 international energy organizations have confirmed their attendance, though it was not clear ⁠whether the participants would attend in person or virtually.
Reuters said a ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to take place, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors.
In addition to attacks on civil aviation, the Houthis have also been trying to choke off oil tanker traffic through the Bab el Mandeb strait, a key entry point to the Red Sea, as Iran has effectively done in the Strait of Hormuz to the north of the Arabian Peninsula.
Earlier this month, Yemeni government forces said they reclaimed the strategic port city of Mokha from the Houthis.
Energy prices have soared since the start of the Iran war, which began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets on Feb. 28, putting pressure on consumers globally.
The surge in domestic fuel prices has been a key issue for voters ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections.
But that support would be expensive militarily.
"Potential U.S. involvement in the Saudi-Yemeni government air campaign to degrade Houthi ballistic missile capabilities would mark the first direct U.S. military action against the group since the conclusion of Operation Rough Rider in May 2025," according to the Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute think tank.
The offensive aimed to suppress the Houthis' capabilities, but recent attacks show the group has regrouped.
"After seven months of war, there are questions about the U.S. capacity to wage a sustained campaign against the Houthis, return to combat against Iran if necessary, and prepare for contingencies in other parts of the world, notably East Asia," Steven Cook, an expert on Arab and Turkish politics at the Council on Foreign Relations think tank, wrote last month.
Meanwhile, the United Kingdom's defense secretary said his government is also examining how to support Saudi Arabia.
"I've spoken to my Saudi counterpart [Khalid bin Salman] on a number of occasions in recent weeks to look at what more we can do to support Saudi Arabia, and I'm afraid last night explains precisely why we are providing that support," Wes Streeting said in an interview on BBC television on Sunday.
Streeting said the U.K. is not getting involved in offensive operations "at this stage."
"We've always been clear that there isn't a military solution to this conflict," Streeting added.

articles.title_orig: She was a global star: Teen bikes 700 miles carrying injured dad. Where is she now?
articles.title_zh: She was a global star: Teen bikes 700 miles carrying injured dad. Where is she now?
articles.content_orig:
Jyoti Kumari holds a photo of her dad, Mohan Paswan. She became a global celebrity after news spread of her 700-mile bicycle ride, carrying her injured father on her bicycle, to get him to their village. Promises were made to reward her heroic feat. Were they kept? Deepak Paswan hide caption
Fame is a strange beast. It brings applause, attention and promises of a better life. But when the spotlight moves on, those promises are often forgotten. No one knows this better than 22-year-old Jyoti Kumari.
When she was 15 years old, during the peak of India's COVID shutdown , she shot to international fame for cycling over 700 miles, from northern India to her village in the eastern state of Bihar, with her injured father riding on the back of the hot pink bike she'd bought for $20.
Her dad, Mohan Paswan, drove an autorickshaw for 20 years in Gurugram, a city near Delhi , sending money to his wife and five children in the village of Sirhulli. After he suffered a debilitating road accident in January 2020, Kumari and her mom took the train to Gurugram to care for him.
Five months later, he still hadn't made a full recovery and his family was running out of money for food and rent. The family decided they would all be better off at home. But at the time, authorities had shut down public transportation for the pandemic lockdown. No one knew how Mohan Paswan could make the journey. That's when Kumari insisted she would bring him back home, riding on a pad attached to the main seat of her bicycle.
She cycled for seven consecutive days on a relatively empty stomach at the height of the lockdown to get him to safety. Even though it was a test of sheer endurance, Kumari discovered that she loved cycling — it came naturally to her.
लॉकडाउन था, सो अपने पिता को साइकिल पर बैठाकर गुरुग्राम से दरभंगा ले गई बेटी... वीडियो: मोहन भारद्वाज और सीटू तिवारी pic.twitter.com/Mc7hkmyB4O
Her epic ride grabbed headlines around the world. NPR's previous reporting noted promises of cash rewards, training for a career as a cyclist, even a movie deal.
That was in 2020. "Now — life is hard," Kumari told NPR in a phone call from her home in Bihar.
What happened to all the promises made — for financial support, especially to support cycling as a competitive sport?
Many promises were not kept, she says.
"The politicians who made promises, saying they would give money for my sports or education — nobody actually gave anything," she says. "Whatever reward money we collected back then [from individuals who extended help and a government award that came with a cash prize], we put it all into our house, rebuilding it. We had a brick house before, but it only had bare walls. Now we have completed it, added a toilet, a bathroom, and a running water connection. By doing all that, the house has finally become livable," she says.
This is no small achievement. An estimated 300,000 people are homeless in the state of Bihar in spite of government programs . For a family living in poverty, having a home can make a huge difference in the fight for survival.
For Kumari's family, making their house livable meant securing something that burst of fame had failed to deliver on — a more stable place from which to build their lives.
But they are doing so without her dad.
Mohan Paswan passed away of a heart attack in May 2021, just months after his daughter brought him home. Kumari says she felt heartbroken. After his passing, financial security has been precarious for the family.
At the moment, her mother works as a cook. Her meager income supports Kumari and her three siblings at home (an older sister has married and moved out).
"There are days when we go to sleep hungry," she says. "Our brother-in-law used to help us earlier, but now he also has a child, a wife and his father to take care of. He works a small job in the city — how much can he really do? So now he isn't able to help us much."
Still she holds out hope for a better future.
"Once my education is fully complete, only then will I be able to do something else. Only then can I prepare for things and look for a job," Kumari says.
But she has yet to pass the final exam required to complete Class 12, her final year of secondary school. That's an important credential to apply to university or qualify for certain jobs. It's a stepping stone to a better life, especially for disadvantaged students.
Finding time for her studies has been a challenge. Kumari's day begins at 7 a.m. She cooks and cares for her younger siblings after her mother rushes off to work. "I give my brothers breakfast for school and get things ready for my sister. Then, I clean the house, mop the floors, do the dishes, wash clothes by hand, take a bath," she says.
By the time she can turn her attention to her studies, she says it feels as if she has already done a gazillion chores. "There are days when I sleep because of the sheer exhaustion of it all."
Whatever the future holds, she is determined to stay in their native village rather than seeking employment in the big city, as her father did. His experience showed her how precarious day labor can be — he had no savings and no medical support after his injury.
Kumari is firm about living in their native village. "Whatever I do, I want to do from here," she says.
She says she still loves cycling as much as ever. She loves the wind in her hair, the feeling of going somewhere, of feeling free. That's what the bike represents to her. But she doesn't have the time to do it as much these days as she's bogged down by household chores and small but persistent everyday worries. She can't just cycle for the joy of it or train as a competitive sport. She only cycles to do errands for the family.
With her own progress on hold, the family has quietly set their hopes on her younger sister who will take her 12th grade exams in mid-2027. If she manages to pass and get into a good college, their prospects will improve once she graduates and starts working.
But Kumari hasn't given up. "When you're poor, fame doesn't help. Only education can help you out of your difficulties. Otherwise, life becomes a never-ending obstacle course," Kumari says.

articles.title_orig: UK does not support Trump's Russia diesel deal, says Streeting
articles.title_zh: UK does not support Trump's Russia diesel deal, says Streeting
articles.content_orig:
The UK does not support Donald Trump's deal with Vladimir Putin, which would see the US purchase millions of tonnes of diesel from Russia, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House, he said the agreement had been done in the context of the US president facing elections in November and at a time when politicians across the world were under pressure to ease the cost of living.
He argued that the US and other allies should focus on increasing pressure on Russia to shorten the war "and to secure Ukraine's freedom".
Trump's diesel deal is aimed at lowering fuel prices in America, which have risen following the US and Israel's conflict with Iran.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the agreement would allow Moscow to raise funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.
In response, Trump suggested Ukraine should "get a new leader" who could reach a deal with Russia to end the long-running conflict between the two countries.
Streeting said it was a matter for Ukrainians to choose their leader but added that the country was "fortunate to have someone of his calibre, his courage and his integrity leading their war effort".
He added that responsibility for the war "lies squarely and solely with President Putin and his imperialist ambitions".
The defence secretary said it was not the first time there had been public disagreements between Washington and Kyiv, adding: "In these situations we see it as our role and our responsibility to try and bring our friends back together again."
He also sought to emphasise the US's support for Ukraine, saying there was "often an understatement" of how much help they had provided.
"We're seeing US support for Ukraine in a number of ways from the provision of weapons - and we do a lot of procurement through the Americans - through to intelligence support and through the diplomatic initiative that Washington is leading."
Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Trump was "wrong" to call for Zelensky to go, adding: "The US is our closest ally but even close allies can disagree."
Speaking on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he also criticised the diesel deal saying it "sends out all the wrong messages".
"If you want a peaceful world, you don't do that sort of deal - you properly fund defence and prepare for war."
Also appearing on the programme, Streeting said the UK had to plan its defence spending on the basis that there could be a Russian attack on Nato - the military alliance made up of 32 countries - by 2030.
He said the UK didn't "seek conflict with Russia" but added: "Strength is the best form of deterrence."
Earlier this year, John Healey - now the chancellor - resigned as defence secretary accusing Sir Keir Starmer's government of not providing enough money for defence and said the UK had to be spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030, up from an estimated 2.6% this year.
Streeting said Healey would use the coming Budget to "plug" a £4.7bn funding gap to pay for the Defence Investment Plan.
He also said the government would set out a path to increase spending to 3.5% of national income by 2035 at next year's Spending Review.
Pressed on whether the government could commit to spending 3% of GDP by 2030, Streeting said he would "always push for more defence spending" but added: "We're not going to set out a spending commitment without showing how we will pay for it."
"If I were the chancellor to sit on your programme now and say '3% in 2030' without saying how we would pay for it, the markets would price in that risk and the cost of borrowing would go up."
